raw: 46.1 ICS Matrix: 12 Tactics, Full Technique Library[^213]
teaching_note: ATT&CK for ICS organizes documented adversary behaviors by tactical objective; it is neither an exhaustive catalog of possible behavior nor a mandatory attack sequence [@ageint213]. This walkthrough is a selected subset: the inspected v20 matrix (6 November 2026; version permalink https://attack.mitre.org/versions/v20/matrices/ics/) has twelve tactics, including Privilege Escalation, concerning higher-level permissions, and Command and Control, concerning communication with compromised systems, which the inherited subsections do not separately enumerate. Neither an administrative permission nor an ordinary communication alone proves those adversary objectives. Record version and technique identity for each mapping: counts and names can change, and a colored matrix cell is not evidence of local detection or prevention.
title: ICS Matrix: Versioned Tactics and Technique Knowledge Base

raw: 46.1.1 Initial Access (12 techniques): Drive-by, Remote Services, Wireless Compromise[^213]
teaching_note: Initial Access describes gaining a foothold, not every use of remote access [@ageint213]. A fictional paper record showing a remote session is compatible with ordinary maintenance; without authorization context it supports only a session observation, not a compromise finding. The inherited count belongs to a matrix snapshot, not a permanent curriculum invariant; no live access or discovery is part of this lesson.
title: Initial Access: Version-dependent Entry-behavior Categories

raw: 46.1.2 Execution: Modify Controller Tasking, Command-Line Interface[^213]
teaching_note: Execution concerns running adversary-controlled activity; the inherited Command-Line Interface label should be reconciled against the pinned matrix, whose inspected v20 uses Command and Scripting Interpreter [@ageint213]. An audit entry containing a tasking-change request does not prove execution, success, or physical effect. Use inert event descriptions to distinguish request, acknowledgment, and execution evidence without supplying commands.
title: Execution: Tasking Changes and Versioned Interpreter Categories

raw: 46.1.3 Persistence: Modify Firmware (System and Module), Project File Infection[^213]
teaching_note: Persistence describes maintaining access or activity, whereas firmware modification and project-file infection describe candidate mechanisms in the knowledge base [@ageint213]. A changed file hash proves a byte difference only when the baseline and comparison are trustworthy; it does not establish malicious purpose, persistence, or controller deployment. Compare supplied fictional version records and approved-change explanations before assigning a technique.
title: Persistence: Modify Firmware (System and Module), Project File Infection

teaching_note: Evasion categories describe concealment or avoidance of defenses, but absent logs alone do not establish deliberate removal [@ageint213]. Ordinary rotation, collection failure, and clock mismatch are competing explanations. Preserve an unknown disposition until an authorized artifact supports the distinguishing behavior; do not reconstruct or demonstrate concealment.
title: Evasion: Rootkit, Masquerading, Indicator Removal

raw: 46.1.5 Discovery: Remote System Discovery, Network Sniffing[^213]
teaching_note: Discovery concerns learning about an environment; the same observable may arise from an approved inventory process [@ageint213]. A classroom analyst classifies already supplied fictional descriptions, not real packets or devices. Permission, timing, and the stated task separate benign inventory from a supported adversary-behavior assessment; no scanning, sniffing, or live connection is authorized.
title: Discovery: Remote System Discovery, Network Sniffing

raw: 46.1.6 Lateral Movement: Lateral Tool Transfer, Valid Accounts[^213]
teaching_note: Lateral Movement concerns movement between systems; a valid account identifies a credential context, not the human who used it [@ageint213]. The presence of an account on two machines does not establish movement or attribution. A candidate mapping needs supplied evidence of the cross-system behavior and a comparison with authorized workflow.
title: Lateral Movement: Lateral Tool Transfer, Valid Accounts

raw: 46.1.7 Collection: I/O Image, Monitor Process State, Point & Tag Identification[^213]
teaching_note: An I/O image represents controller-associated input/output state; process-state and tag observations concern operational meaning rather than just network identifiers [@ageint213]. Reading such data can be routine supervision, so a collection mapping requires evidence of the relevant adversary behavior. A tag name alone may not establish its units, sensor lineage, or physical role; those remain missing process context.
title: Collection: I/O Image, Monitor Process State, Point & Tag Identification

raw: 46.1.8 Inhibit Response Function: Alarm Suppression, Block Communications[^213]
teaching_note: Inhibiting a response function concerns interference with protective or responsive functions, not merely the observation of a quiet alarm feed [@ageint213]. In a synthetic paper case, card A has two missing messages and card B states maintenance: the mapping row is 'candidate T0878 Alarm Suppression / ATT&CK ICS v20; supporting observation A; alternative B; attack confidence low; direct alarm-configuration evidence absent; reviewer hold'. When corrected maintenance card B2 accounts for both messages, the candidate adversarial mapping is withdrawn as a benign-change negative control. No independent evidence establishes suppression, so the reviewer stops escalation of the attack claim and issues no device action; a new authorized record demonstrating relevant interference would reopen the assessment, not trigger an automatic response.
title: Inhibit Response Function: Alarm Suppression, Block Communications

raw: 46.1.9 Impair Process Control: Brute Force I/O, Modify Parameter[^213]
teaching_note: Impair Process Control concerns disruption or manipulation of control functions; a parameter difference is not automatically an unsafe state [@ageint213]. Its significance depends on units, operating mode, approved limits, and the process at that time. This lesson evaluates fictional evidence descriptions only and supplies no parameter values for devices, actuation steps, or unsafe simulation.
title: Impair Process Control: Brute Force I/O, Modify Parameter

raw: 46.1.10 Impact: Damage to Property, Loss of Safety, Manipulation of Control[^213]
teaching_note: Impact categories name adversary objectives or reported consequences, not effects established by every preceding technique [@ageint213]. Loss of view, loss of control, and physical damage are distinct claims requiring distinct evidence. An alert or a candidate technique mapping cannot by itself establish injury, equipment damage, or safety-system failure.
title: Impact: Damage to Property, Loss of Safety, Manipulation of Control

raw: 46.2 Using ICS ATT&CK in Risk Assessment (ISA InTech)[^214]
teaching_note: A technique map helps ask what behavior matters for a specified architecture; it does not supply the likelihood of compromise or severity of a physical consequence [@ageint214]. Distinguish 'mapped' (a proposed taxonomy association), 'observable in supplied data' (the required evidence exists), 'tested in this fixture' (a bounded demonstration), 'untested', 'unknown' (insufficient evidence), and 'not applicable' (an explained scope exclusion). Compare the behavior, required observable, available sensor coverage, and relevant process dependency before choosing a disposition. Unsupported combinations remain gaps, not zero risk or proof of inevitable harm.
title: Using ICS ATT&CK in Risk Assessment (ISA InTech)

raw: 46.3 Dragos: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS Threat Actor Mapping[^215]
teaching_note: A vendor mapping associates reported behavior with its analytic group labels; technique overlap alone cannot identify an actor [@ageint215]. Record whether a statement is the vendor's assessment, a quoted observation, or this manuscript's inference. Several reports reusing one underlying incident do not create independent attribution support.
title: Dragos: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS Threat Actor Mapping

raw: 46.4 Nozomi Networks: How Security Teams Use the ICS Framework[^216]
teaching_note: Vendor instruction can illustrate framework use without establishing comparative control efficacy [@ageint216]. Separate documented mapping coverage, installed observation capability, demonstrated detection in a bounded fixture, and prevention of real process harm. None of these follows automatically from the preceding category; use Section [@sec:analytic-workflow] for a claim record that preserves that boundary.
title: Nozomi Networks: How Security Teams Use the ICS Framework
